Dit artikel onderzoekt de geldigheid van deze claims door beschikbare wetenschappelijke bewijsmateriaal, officiële verklaringen en de aard van mRNA-vaccins te beoordelen.

**Achtergrond over mRNA-vaccins en het spike-eiwit**

Pfizer's COVID-19-vaccin, net als andere mRNA-vaccins, werkt door genetische instructies (mRNA) aan cellen te leveren, die vervolgens een onschadelijk versie van het spike-eiwit produceren dat zich op de oppervlakte van het SARS-CoV-2-virus bevindt. Hierdoor kan het immuunsysteem herkennen en reageren op het echte virus als het wordt tegengekomen. Het spike-eiwit dat door het vaccin wordt geproduceerd blijft binnen het lichaam van de gevaccineerde persoon en is geen volledig virus, dus het kan geen COVID-19 veroorzaken.

**Claim 1: Overdraagbaarheid van het spike-eiwit**

De sociale media-post stelt dat Pfizer erkent dat het door het vaccin gegenereerde spike-eiwit overdraagbaar is aan anderen. Deze claim lijkt af te leiden van een misinterpretatie van een document dat betrekking heeft op Pfizer's klinische toetsingsprotocollen, waarin onderzoekers werden opgedragen om te monitoren op mogelijke "expositie" van het vaccin bij mensen in directe nabijheid, zoals via huidcontact of inademing. Echter, dit was een voorzorgsmaatregel die gebruikelijk was in vroege ontwerp van nieuwe geneesmiddelen, niet een erkentenis dat het spike-eiwit of mRNA overdraagbaar is van persoon op persoon.

Er is geen wetenschappelijk bewijs dat het spike-eiwit of het mRNA dat ervoor codeert, wordt afgestoten door gevaccineerde personen op een manier die overdraagbaar is aan anderen. Het mRNA en de daaruit ontstane eiwitten worden snel in het lichaam afgebroken. De begrip van "vaccinverlies" is relevant voor sommige levende, verzwakte vaccins, maar niet van toepassing op mRNA-vaccins, die geen levend virus bevatten.

**Claim 2: Spike-eiwit en bloedstolsels**

De post stelt ook dat Pfizer erkent dat documentatie bestaat die aantoont dat het spike-eiwit bloedstolsels kan veroorzaken. Hoewel het waar is dat COVID-19 zelf, en mogelijk het spike-eiwit in het kader van een natuurlijke infectie, een verhoogde risico op bloedstolsels kan opleveren, is de situatie met het vaccin anders. Onderzoek en post-marketing surveillance hebben aangetoond dat het Pfizer mRNA-vaccin een zeer lage kans op bloedstolsels associeert, aanzienlijk lager dan het risico dat wordt geassocieerd met een COVID-19-infectie.

Pfizer heeft geen erkentenis gedaan in officiële documenten dat het door zijn vaccin gegenereerde spike-eiwit bloedstolsels veroorzaakt. Wereldwijde regelgevers, waaronder de FDA en de EMA, hebben de veiligheidsdata grondig bekeken en hebben geen bewijs gevonden dat het spike-eiwit dat na vaccinatie wordt geproduceerd aanzienlijke bloedstolselrisico's oplevert bij de algemene bevolking.

**Conclusie**

De claims in de sociale media-post worden niet gesteund door bewijs. Er is geen aanduiding in Pfizer's officiële documenten dat het spike-eiwit van zijn mRNA-vaccin overdraagbaar is aan anderen, noch is er een erkentenis of documentatie die aantoont dat het door het vaccin gegenereerde spike-eiwit bloedstolsels veroorzaakt. Deze uitspraken vertegenwoordigen de werking van mRNA-vaccins en de beschikbare wetenschappelijke gegevens over vaccinveiligheid onjuist.

According to the post, the nurse allegedly emptied the contents of the vaccine on the ground rather than injecting it into Hopkins, suggesting that the vaccination was staged or faked.

To evaluate this claim, it is important to consider both the context of Anthony Hopkins’ vaccination and the broader environment of COVID-19 vaccine skepticism.

Anthony Hopkins, the acclaimed actor, publicly shared his COVID-19 vaccination experience in January 2021, posting a video on his social media accounts. The video showed him sitting in his car and receiving a vaccine injection from a nurse through the car window. This video was widely shared and became one of several high-profile celebrity vaccination moments aimed at encouraging public trust in the vaccine rollout during the pandemic.

The core claim in the social media post hinges on the allegation that the nurse did not actually inject the vaccine, but instead disposed of it on the ground. This is a type of conspiracy theory that has surfaced repeatedly during the COVID-19 vaccination campaign, often targeting celebrities and public figures. Such claims typically rely on grainy videos, misinterpretation of camera angles, or lack of visible fluid in syringes to suggest that vaccinations are being staged.

Upon reviewing the available video and photographic evidence of Anthony Hopkins’ vaccination, there is no credible indication that the nurse emptied the vaccine on the ground. The video shows the nurse preparing the syringe and injecting Hopkins in his upper arm through an open car window. There is no visible evidence in the footage to support the assertion that the contents were discarded or not administered. While the video does not provide a close-up view of the syringe or the nurse’s hands at every moment, this is standard for most vaccination documentation, and not unusual or suspicious in itself.

Additionally, there have been no credible reports, from Hopkins himself, the vaccination site, or health authorities, to suggest that the vaccination was staged or faked. Hopkins has publicly expressed gratitude for receiving the vaccine and encouraged others to do the same, consistent with the goals of public health messaging at the time.

It is also important to note that accusations like this can undermine public confidence in vaccination and health authorities. Health care workers administering vaccines during the pandemic have been under significant scrutiny, and there is no evidence to suggest a pattern of staged vaccinations among celebrities or the general public.

In conclusion, the claim that the nurse administering the COVID-19 vaccine to Anthony Hopkins emptied the contents of the syringe on the ground, rather than properly vaccinating him, is not supported by any credible evidence. The available video footage does not corroborate this allegation, and it appears to be part of a broader pattern of misinformation surrounding COVID-19 vaccines and public figures.

article_content:
A social media post circulating online claims that, according to Johns Hopkins University, COVID-19 vaccines have been designed in such a way that vaccinated people can transmit the virus to others they come into contact with. This statement raises concerns about the function and safety of COVID-19 vaccines and the intentions behind their development. To clarify the facts, it is important to examine the scientific basis for the claim, the intended purpose of COVID-19 vaccines, and what institutions like Johns Hopkins University have actually communicated about vaccine transmission.

COVID-19 vaccines—including those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, Johnson & Johnson, and others—were designed to protect individuals against severe disease, hospitalization, and death caused by SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. These vaccines work primarily by stimulating the immune system to recognize and fight the virus if the vaccinated person is exposed in the future. The main goal has been to reduce severe outcomes, though many vaccines also reduce the risk of infection and transmission to some degree.

The assertion that COVID-19 vaccines were "designed" to allow vaccinated individuals to transmit the virus is misleading. No credible scientific body, including Johns Hopkins University, has stated or implied that vaccines were intentionally created to facilitate transmission. In fact, vaccine development efforts have focused on providing robust protection and, where possible, reducing the spread of the virus.

It is true, however, that breakthrough infections—cases where vaccinated individuals contract COVID-19—can occur. In such cases, vaccinated individuals may transmit the virus to others, particularly if they are symptomatic. This possibility was recognized by researchers and public health officials, especially as new variants like Delta and Omicron emerged, which demonstrated increased transmissibility and some ability to evade immune protection. However, the fact that transmission can occur among vaccinated individuals does not mean the vaccines were designed for this purpose; rather, it reflects the evolving nature of the virus and the limitations of existing vaccines.

Johns Hopkins University, along with other leading health institutions, has provided public guidance acknowledging that while COVID-19 vaccines are highly effective at reducing severe illness and death, they do not guarantee complete protection against infection or transmission. This is common with many vaccines, especially those targeting respiratory viruses. For instance, people who receive the flu vaccine can occasionally still contract and transmit influenza, but the vaccine remains a critical tool for minimizing the impact of the virus.

In summary, the claim that COVID-19 vaccines were designed so that vaccinated people can transmit the virus to others misrepresents the purpose and function of these vaccines. While vaccinated individuals can sometimes transmit COVID-19, especially with highly transmissible variants, this is a limitation of current vaccine technology, not a deliberate design feature. The overwhelming consensus among scientists and public health experts is that COVID-19 vaccines were developed to protect individuals and communities from the worst effects of the disease, not to encourage transmission. It is crucial for the public to rely on accurate information from reputable sources when evaluating claims about vaccine safety and effectiveness.

ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ, ਵਾਸਤਵਿਕ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ, ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਕੋਵਿਡ-19 ਲੈਣ ਦੀ ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਹੋ ਸਕਦੀ ਹੈ। ਇਸ ਕੇਸ ਵਿੱਚ, ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਲੋਕ ਹੋਰ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਫੈਲਾ ਸਕਦੇ ਹਨ, ਖ਼ਾਸ ਕਰਕੇ ਜੇ ਉਹ ਲੱਛਣ ਵਾਲੇ ਹੋਣ। ਇਸ ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਨੂੰ ਵਿਗਿਆਨੀਆਂ ਅਤੇ ਸਾਂਝੇ ਸਿਹਤ ਅਧਿਕਾਰੀਆਂ ਨੇ ਪਛਾਲੇ ਸਮੇਂ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ, ਖ਼ਾਸ ਕਰਕੇ ਜੇ ਨਵੇਂ ਵੈਰੀਐਂਟ ਜਿਵੇਂ ਡੈਲਟਾ ਅਤੇ ਓਮੀਕਰੰ ਨੂੰ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੀ ਫੈਲਾਉਣ ਦੀ ਸਮਰੱਥਾ ਅਤੇ ਕੁਝ ਤਰ੍ਹਾਂ ਇਮਿਊਨ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੈਕਸ਼ਨ ਨੂੰ ਭੰਗ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਸਮਰੱਥਾ ਵਾਲੇ ਬਾਰੇ ਮੰਨਿਆ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ। ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ, ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਲੋਕ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਫੈਲਾਉਣ ਦੀ ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਹੋ ਸਕਦੀ ਹੈ ਇਸ ਤੱਥ ਨੂੰ ਕਿ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਨੂੰ ਇਸ ਦੇ ਲਈ ਵਿਕਸਿਤ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ ਦੱਸਣ ਲਈ ਗਲਤ ਹੈ; ਬਜਾਏ ਇਸ ਦੇ, ਇਹ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੇ ਬਦਲਾਵ ਅਤੇ ਵਰਤੇ ਗਏ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੇ ਸੀਮਾਵਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਦਰਸਾਉਂਦਾ ਹੈ।

ਜੋਹਨਸ਼ਪਿੰਗ ਯੂਨੀਵਰਸਿਟੀ, ਸਾਂਝੇ ਸਿਹਤ ਸੰਸਥਾਵਾਂ ਨਾਲ ਮਿਲ ਕੇ, ਇਸ ਦੀ ਸਾਂਝੇ ਮਾਰਗਦਰਸ਼ਨ ਪੇਸ਼ ਕਰਦੀ ਹੈ ਜਿਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਕਿਹਾ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ ਕੋਵਿਡ-19 ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਗੰਭੀਰ ਬਿਮਾਰੀ ਅਤੇ ਮੌਤ ਨੂੰ ਘੱਟ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਬਹੁਤ ਕੁਸ਼ਲ ਹੈ, ਇਸ ਨੂੰ ਸੰਪਰਕ ਅਤੇ ਫੈਲਾਉਣ ਦੇ ਲਈ ਪੂਰੀ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਪ੍ਰਦਾਨ ਨਹੀਂ ਕਰਦੀ। ਇਹ ਹੈ ਸਾਂਝੇ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਵਸਤੂ, ਖ਼ਾਸ ਕਰਕੇ ਜੋ ਸੰਸਥਾਵਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਦਿਮਾਗੀ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਨੂੰ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਹਨ। ਉਦਾਹਰਨ ਲਈ, ਫਲੂ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਲੋਕ ਕਦੇ-ਕਦੇ ਫਲੂ ਨੂੰ ਲੈ ਸਕਦੇ ਹਨ ਅਤੇ ਫੈਲਾ ਸਕਦੇ ਹਨ, ਪਰ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਦੇ ਪ੍ਰਭਾਵ ਨੂੰ ਘੱਟ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਮਹੱਤਵਪੂਰਨ ਉਪਕਰਣ ਹੈ।

ਇਸ ਨੂੰ ਸੰਕਲਨ ਕਰਦੇ ਹੋਏ, ਕੋਵਿਡ-19 ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਨੂੰ ਵਿਕਸਿਤ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ ਤਾਂ ਕਿ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਲੋਕ ਹੋਰ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਵਾਇਰਸ ਫੈਲਾ ਸਕਣ ਦਾ ਦਾਅਵਾ ਕਰਨਾ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੇ ਉਦੇਸ਼ ਅਤੇ ਕੰਮ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਸੰਸਥਾ ਨੂੰ ਗਲਤ ਤਰੀਕੇ ਨਾਲ ਵੱਲ ਇਸ਼ਾਰਾ ਕਰਦਾ ਹੈ। ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ, ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਲੈਂਦੇ ਲੋਕ ਕਦੇ-ਕਦੇ ਕੋਵਿਡ-19 ਲੈ ਸਕਦੇ ਹਨ, ਖ਼ਾਸ ਕਰਕੇ ਬਹੁਤ ਸੰਪਰਕ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੇ ਵੈਰੀਐਂਟ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ, ਇਹ ਹੈ ਵਰਤੇ ਗਏ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਤਕਨੋਲੋਜੀ ਦੀ ਸੀਮਾ, ਨਾ ਕਿ ਇਸ ਦੇ ਨਿਯੋਜਨ ਦਾ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਹੈ। ਵਿਗਿਆਨੀਆਂ ਅਤੇ ਸਾਂਝੇ ਸਿਹਤ ਵਿਗਿਆਨੀਆਂ ਦੇ ਬਹੁਤ ਵੱਡੇ ਮੁੱਕੇ ਹਨ ਕਿ ਕੋਵਿਡ-19 ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਨੂੰ ਵਿਕਸਿਤ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ ਤਾਂ ਵਿਅਕਤੀਆਂ ਅਤੇ ਸਮੂਹਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਰੋਗ ਦੇ ਖ਼ਤਰੇ ਨੂੰ ਘੱਟ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ, ਨਹੀਂ ਕਿ ਫੈਲਾਉਣ ਨੂੰ ਉਤਸ਼ਾਹਿਤ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ। ਸਾਂਝੇ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਦੀ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਲਈ ਸ਼ਾਨਦਾਰ ਸੰਸਥਾਵਾਂ ਨੂੰ ਮੁੱਲੀ ਜਾਣਕਾਰੀ ਨੂੰ ਵਰਤਣਾ ਮਹੱਤਵਪੂਰਨ ਹੈ ਜਦੋਂ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਅਤੇ ਕੁਸ਼ਲਤਾ ਬਾਰੇ ਕਹਾਣੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ ਕਰਦੇ ਹਨ।
article_summary: A social media claim suggests COVID-19 vaccines were designed to allow vaccinated individuals to transmit the virus, but this misrepresents their purpose. Vaccines aim to prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death, with some reducing infection and transmission risk. Experts clarify that while breakthrough infections can occur, especially with new variants, vaccines were not designed to facilitate transmission, and such cases reflect viral evolution, not intentional vaccine design.

A recent social media post has sparked debate by claiming that Dr. Vasilis Vasilakopoulos, a pulmonologist, stated that anyone who does get vaccinated should pay big fines. This statement, if true, would represent a contentious stance, especially considering the ongoing global efforts to promote COVID-19 vaccination. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine both Dr. Vasilakopoulos’s public statements and the broader context of the vaccination debate.

Dr. Vasilis Vasilakopoulos is a well-known Greek pulmonologist and professor at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens. He has been a frequent commentator on public health matters during the COVID-19 pandemic, often appearing in Greek media to advocate for vaccination as a primary tool in controlling the spread of the virus and reducing the severity of illness.

The social media post alleges that Dr. Vasilakopoulos suggested that those who get vaccinated should be subject to substantial fines. This claim appears to invert the more commonly discussed policy proposals, which have revolved around imposing penalties or restrictions on those who remain unvaccinated, rather than those who choose to get vaccinated. In several countries, including Greece, there have been discussions and implementations of fines or social restrictions for unvaccinated individuals, particularly among vulnerable populations such as the elderly.

A review of recent media coverage and public statements by Dr. Vasilakopoulos reveals that he has been a strong proponent of vaccination and has, on occasion, advocated for stricter measures to encourage vaccine uptake. For example, he has publicly supported fines or additional restrictions for adults who refuse vaccination without valid medical reasons, arguing that such measures protect public health and reduce the strain on healthcare systems.

There is no evidence, however, to suggest that Dr. Vasilakopoulos has ever called for fines to be levied on those who receive the vaccine. On the contrary, his public statements have consistently encouraged vaccination and framed it as a civic duty. The claim in the social media post appears to be a misrepresentation or possibly a misinterpretation of his actual position. In some cases, controversial statements can be taken out of context or altered in translation, but a thorough search yields no record of Dr. Vasilakopoulos expressing the opinion attributed to him in the post.

In conclusion, the core claim of the social media post—that Dr. Vasilakopoulos advocated for fining vaccinated individuals—is not supported by available evidence. Dr. Vasilakopoulos’s public statements and professional stance have been in favor of vaccination and, if anything, in favor of stronger incentives or penalties targeting those who refuse vaccination. article_content:
A recent social media post claims that the “Center Territorial d’Information Pharmaceutique d’Avis” (CTIAP) has officially demanded a halt to the use of all four COVID-19 vaccines approved in Europe, asserting that none of them are safe or effective. This assertion, which has circulated widely online, has raised concern and confusion about the status of COVID-19 vaccine safety and oversight in Europe. Here, we examine the claim in detail and provide context regarding the organization, the vaccines, and the official positions of relevant authorities.

First, it is important to clarify what the CTIAP is and its role in public health. The CTIAP, or Centre Territorial d’Information Indépendante et d’Avis Pharmaceutiques, is a local entity based in Cholet, France. Its function is to provide independent pharmaceutical information and advice at a regional healthcare facility. The CTIAP is not a regulatory body; it does not have the authority to make binding recommendations or demands regarding the approval, suspension, or withdrawal of medicines or vaccines at the national or European level. Decisions about the approval and safety of vaccines in Europe are made by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national health authorities.

The claim that the CTIAP made an “official demand” to stop COVID-19 vaccines stems from a document published by the organization in April 2021. This document raised concerns about the processes used for the conditional approval of COVID-19 vaccines and suggested that further studies and data collection were necessary. However, the document did not constitute a formal demand or directive to halt vaccination campaigns. Instead, it reflected the opinions of the CTIAP team and was not endorsed by any regulatory or governmental body.

Furthermore, the assertion that “none” of the four COVID-19 vaccines approved in Europe are safe or effective contradicts the current scientific consensus and the ongoing monitoring conducted by regulatory agencies. The EMA, which is responsible for the scientific evaluation, supervision, and safety monitoring of medicines in the European Union, has repeatedly reviewed the safety and efficacy data for all COVID-19 vaccines authorized in the EU, including those from Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, AstraZeneca, and Johnson & Johnson. The agency’s ongoing assessments have found that the benefits of these vaccines in preventing COVID-19 and its complications outweigh the risks of side effects for the vast majority of people.

It is natural for scientific and medical organizations to call for continued monitoring and transparency, especially with new vaccines developed under expedited conditions. Post-authorization studies and pharmacovigilance are standard practice, and rare side effects are continually evaluated. However, such caution does not equate to an official call to halt the use of vaccines, nor does it mean that existing data demonstrate a lack of safety or effectiveness.

In summary, the social media claim misrepresents both the authority and the statements of the CTIAP, as well as the established safety and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines approved in Europe. Regulatory agencies continue to recommend vaccination as a safe and effective means of controlling the COVID-19 pandemic, and decisions regarding vaccine usage remain grounded in ongoing scientific evaluation.

Artikel:
Sebuah post media sosial baru-baru ini menyatakan bahawa "Pusat Kebangsaan Maklumat Farmasi dan Pandangan" (CTIAP) telah secara rasmi meminta penghentian penggunaan semua empat vaksin COVID-19 yang telah diluluskan di Eropah, menyatakan bahawa tidak satu pun daripadanya selamat atau berkesan. Pernyataan ini, yang telah berpindah luas di internet, telah menimbulkan kebimbangan dan kekeliruan mengenai status keselamatan dan pengawasan vaksin COVID-19 di Eropah. Di sini, kita akan mengkaji klaim tersebut secara terperinci dan memberikan konteks mengenai organisasi, vaksin, serta pendirian rasmi pihak berkuasa yang relevan.

Pertama, penting untuk memahami apakah CTIAP itu dan perananannya dalam kesihatan awam. CTIAP, atau Pusat Kebangsaan Maklumat Farmasi dan Pandangan yang Berindependensi, merupakan sebuah entiti tempatan yang berpangkalan di Cholet, Perancis. Fungsinya ialah menyediakan maklumat farmasi dan nasihat yang bebas di sebuah fasiliti kesihatan awam daerah. CTIAP bukanlah sebuah badan pemerintah; ia tidak mempunyai kuasa untuk membuat rekomendasi atau arahan yang mengikat mengenai pemberian kebenaran, penangguhan, atau penarikan kembali ubat atau vaksin pada peringkat nasional atau Eropah. Keputusan mengenai pemberian kebenaran dan keselamatan vaksin di Eropah dibuat oleh Lembaga Farmasi Eropah (EMA) serta pihak berkuasa kesihatan nasional.

Klaim bahawa CTIAP telah membuat "permintaan rasmi" untuk menghentikan vaksin COVID-19 berasal daripada sebuah dokumen yang diterbitkan oleh organisasi tersebut pada April 2021. Dokumen ini menyatakan kebimbangan mengenai proses yang digunakan untuk pemberian kebenaran bersyarat vaksin COVID-19 dan menyarankan bahawa kajian lanjut serta pengumpulan data diperlukan. Namun, dokumen tersebut tidak merupakan satu permintaan rasmi atau arahan untuk menghentikan program pengurusan vaksin. Sebaliknya, ia mencerminkan pandangan pasukan CTIAP dan tidak disokong oleh sebarang badan pemerintah atau pengawasan.

Selain itu, pernyataan bahawa "tidak satu pun" daripada empat vaksin COVID-19 yang diluluskan di Eropah selamat atau berkesan bertentangan dengan konsensus sains semasa serta pengawasan yang terus berjalan oleh agensi pemerintah. Lembaga Farmasi Eropah (EMA), yang bertanggungjawab menilai sains, pengawasan, dan pemantauan keselamatan ubat dalam Kesatuan Eropah, telah meninjau ulang berulang kali data keselamatan dan keberkesanan untuk semua vaksin COVID-19 yang diluluskan di Eropah, termasuk vaksin dari Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, AstraZeneca, dan Johnson & Johnson. Penilaian terus-menerus oleh agensi ini telah menunjukkan bahawa manfaat vaksin ini dalam mencegah COVID-19 dan komplikasinya melebihi risiko kesan sampingan untuk kebanyakan orang.

Pada keadaan normal, organisasi sains dan perubatan akan menyeru terus memantau dan memperlihatkan transparansi, terutamanya dengan vaksin baru yang dikembangkan di bawah keadaan yang dipercepatkan. Kajian selepas pemberian kebenaran dan farmakovigilans merupakan amalan standard, dan kesan sampingan yang jarang berlaku terus dinilai. Namun, kesedaran ini tidak bermakna satu seruan rasmi untuk menghentikan penggunaan vaksin, atau bermakna data yang wujud menunjukkan ketiadaan keselamatan atau keberkesanan.

Secara keseluruhannya, klaim media sosial ini menyalahguna kedaulatan dan pernyataan CTIAP, serta keselamatan dan keberkesanan vaksin COVID-19 yang telah diluluskan di Eropah. Agensi pemerintah terus menasihati penggunaan vaksin sebagai kaedah selamat dan berkesan untuk mengawal pandemik COVID-19, dan keputusan mengenai penggunaan vaksin masih berpandukan penilaian sains yang berterusan.

In recent days, a viral social media post has accused the Mayor of Athens, Konstantinos Bakogiannis, of staging his COVID-19 vaccination. The claim centers around a photograph allegedly showing Bakogiannis receiving the vaccine while the syringe used on him still had its protective cap attached. This has led to widespread speculation and skepticism about the authenticity of the mayor’s vaccination, with some suggesting that the event was orchestrated as a public relations stunt rather than a genuine immunization effort.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is essential to consider the context in which public vaccinations by political figures have occurred, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Across Europe and the world, leaders have received their vaccines publicly to encourage citizens to follow suit, aiming to dispel hesitancy and build public trust in the vaccination process. In Greece, where vaccine rollout faced both logistical and public confidence challenges, such events served a symbolic purpose.

The photograph in question, widely shared online, shows Mayor Bakogiannis seated while a healthcare worker appears to administer a vaccine injection into his upper arm. Upon closer inspection, some social media users noted that the syringe seemed to retain a blue or white cap on its needle, leading to the assertion that the vaccination was staged and that no actual injection took place.

Fact-checking this claim requires a careful analysis of the visual evidence and an understanding of medical procedures. First, it is important to acknowledge that syringes used for vaccinations are typically fitted with a protective cap to maintain sterility before use. The cap is removed immediately prior to injection. In the rapid environment of a public event, it is possible that an image could capture a moment before the cap was removed or during the preparation phase, which could be misconstrued as the actual injection.

Furthermore, video footage and additional photographs from the event should be reviewed to determine whether the mayor did, in fact, receive the vaccine. In many cases, a single frame may not provide a complete picture, and subsequent images may show the cap removed and the injection administered properly. Public health authorities and the mayor’s office have consistently stated that Bakogiannis was vaccinated, in line with protocols followed for other public figures.

It is also noteworthy that similar rumors have circulated about other politicians and celebrities worldwide, often fueled by mistrust or misinformation. Such claims typically arise from misinterpretations of photographic evidence or deliberate attempts to undermine public health initiatives.

In conclusion, while the photograph shared on social media appears to show a syringe with a protective cap, there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that Mayor Bakogiannis staged his vaccination or that no injection took place. The context of public vaccinations and the review of available images suggest that the accusation is based on a misunderstanding of the sequence of events during the procedure. Without definitive proof of wrongdoing, the claim remains unsubstantiated and should be viewed with skepticism. It is critical for both media and the public to approach such allegations with caution and to seek comprehensive evidence before drawing conclusions about the integrity of public health actions.

В последни дни, вирулен социјален медија пост го обвинува градоначалникот на Атина, Константинос Бакогијанис, за измама на неговата вакцинација против КОВИД-19. Оваа тврдење се фокусира на фотографијата која се тврди дека покажува Бакогијанис да го прима вакцината, додека шприцовот што го користел ја имал покривачката капка. Ова е довело до широка спекулација и сумња за авеноста на вакцинацијата на градоначалникот, со некои да предлажат дека се случило како публично преследување наместо како истина имунизација.

За да се процени валидноста на оваа тврдење, е важно да се земе предвид контекстот во кој публични вакцинација од политички лица се случиле, особено во текот на пандемијата КОВИД-19. Низ Европа и светот, лидерите се вакцинирале публично за да ги подтикнат граѓаните да го направат истото, со цел да се отстрани сумњата и да се изгради доверба во вакцинацијата. Во Грција, каде што вакцинацијата имаше и логистички и публични доверби прашања, такви настани имаше символична цел.

Фотографијата на прашање, широко споделена на интернет, прикажува градоначалникот Бакогијанис седеа, додека здравственик изгледа да му врзеше вакцина во раменото. При детален преглед, некои корисници на социјални мрежи забележале дека шприцот изгледа да имал син или бели капка на иглата, што доведе до тврдење дека вакцинацијата е измамена и дека не се случила никаква инјекција.

Проверка на оваа тврдење захтева внимателен анализа на визуелниот доказ и разбирање на медицински процеси. Прво, е важно да се признае дека шприцовите што се користат за вакцинација обично се опремени со покривачка капка за да се задржи стерилноста пред користење. Капката се отстранува моментално пред инјекција. Во брзата средина на публична настани, е можно да се застапи моментот пред отстранувањето на капката или во фазата на припрема, што може да се превеличава како истинската инјекција.

Потребно е да се прегледа и видеото и дополнителни фотографии од настаниот за да се определи дали градоначалникот наистина ја добил вакцината. Во многу случаи, еден фрек може да не даде потпун слика, а последовачки слики може да покажуваат капката отстранета и инјекцијата дадена правилно. Авторитети за јавно здравство и управата на градоначалникот настојуваат дека Бакогијанис бил вакциниран, во согласност со протоколите што се следеле за други публични личности.

Со оглед на тоа, исто така е приметно дека слични измани се распространиле за други политичари и звездници низ светот, често подтикнати од недоверба или несигурност. Такви тврдења често се појавуваат од неправилно интерпретирање на фотографскиот доказ или намерен опит да се оспори јавни здравствени иницијативи.

В заклучок, докажувањето на фотографијата споделена на социјални мрежи изгледа како шприц со покривачка капка, нема доволно докази да се поддржи тврдењето дека градоначалникот Бакогијанис измамил вакцинацијата или дека не се случила инјекција. Контекстот на публична вакцинација и прегледот на достапните слики предлажат дека тврдењето е базирано на неправилно разбирање на редоследот на настани во процедурата. Без одреден доказ за нечестност, тврдењето останува неподдржано и треба да се гледа со сумња. Критичен е и за медијите и за јавноста да се однесуваат со такви обвинувања со предпоставка и да трагаат за комплетен доказ пред да извршат заклучоки за интегритетот на јавни здравствени акции.

Οι αρμόδιοι υπογράμμισαν ότι ο δήμαρχος εμβολιάστηκε σύμφωνα με τα πρωτόκολλα, ενώ η συγκεκριμένη εικόνα μπορεί να αντιπροσωπεύει μια στιγμή πριν από την ενέση.

article_content:
A social media post claims that, according to official European Union (EU) data, there had been 10,570 deaths and 405,259 cases of side effects from the COVID-19 vaccines as of May 19th, 2021. The post implies that these figures represent confirmed vaccine-related deaths and side effects, raising concerns about vaccine safety. This article examines the accuracy of these claims, providing context about vaccine safety monitoring and the interpretation of adverse event reports.

The figures referenced in the post likely originate from EudraVigilance, the pharmacovigilance system operated by the European Medicines Agency (EMA), which collects and analyzes reports of suspected adverse reactions to medicines authorized in the European Economic Area (EEA), including vaccines. During the COVID-19 vaccine rollout, EudraVigilance published regular summaries of adverse events reported after vaccination, including both non-serious and serious outcomes, such as death.

It is important to understand how these data are collected and what they represent. EudraVigilance is a passive reporting system, meaning anyone—healthcare professionals, patients, or members of the public—can submit a report of any medical event occurring after vaccination. However, the existence of a report does not mean that the vaccine caused the reported event. These are "suspected" adverse events, and causality is not established at the time of reporting. Many factors can contribute to adverse events, including underlying health conditions, coincidental illnesses, or unrelated causes.

The claim cites 10,570 deaths and 405,259 side effects up to May 19th, 2021. These numbers reflect the total reports submitted to EudraVigilance describing deaths and other side effects following vaccination, not confirmed cases of vaccine-induced harm. By May 2021, hundreds of millions of vaccine doses had been administered across the EU, primarily to older adults and those with underlying health conditions, groups at higher risk for medical events, including death, regardless of vaccination.

Regulatory agencies, including the EMA, rigorously review the data from EudraVigilance and other sources to identify patterns suggesting a causal link between vaccination and specific adverse events. Most reports are found to be coincidental and not caused by the vaccine. When a potential safety signal is detected, further investigation is conducted, and recommendations may be updated. For instance, rare cases of blood clotting with certain vaccines were identified and addressed with guidance, but the overwhelming evidence supported the safety and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines for the general population.

In summary, the figures cited in the social media post are accurate in terms of raw reports submitted to the EU's monitoring system by May 19th, 2021. However, the claim is misleading because these numbers do not represent confirmed vaccine-related deaths or side effects. The vast majority of reported events are not causally linked to vaccination. COVID-19 vaccines underwent extensive clinical trials and continuous monitoring, with regulatory authorities concluding that their benefits far outweigh the risks. Public understanding of vaccine safety should be based on comprehensive scientific assessment, not raw reporting figures.

സോഷ്യൽ മീഡിയയിൽ പോസ്റ്റ് ചെയ്യപ്പെട്ടതനുസരിച്ച്, യൂറോപ്പിയൻ യൂണിയൻ (EU) നിലവിലുള്ള ഡാറ്റയിൽ വാക്സിൻ കൊണ്ട് ഉണ്ടായ മരണങ്ങളുടെ എണ്ണം 10,570 ആയിരുന്നു, കൂടാതെ വാക്സിനുകളുടെ പക്ഷേപങ്ങളുടെ എണ്ണം 405,259 ആയിരുന്നു എന്ന് പറയുന്നു. ഈ ഡാറ്റ വാക്സിൻ ബന്ധിച്ച മരണങ്ങൾ ഉണ്ടായിട്ടുള്ളതാണെന്ന് കരുതിയെങ്കിലും ഇത് വാക്സിനുകളുടെ സുരക്ഷിതത ഉള്ളതാണെന്ന് പ്രശ്നമായിരുന്നു. ഈ വാർത്തയിൽ ഈ പ്രസ്താവനകളുടെ സത്യസന്ധത പരിശോധിക്കുകയും, വാക്സിനുകളുടെ സുരക്ഷിതത പരിശോധനയുടെ പശ്ചാത്തലവും അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ പരിശോധനയുടെ വിശദീകരണവും നൽകുകയും ചെയ്യുന്നു.

പോസ്റ്റിൽ ഉദ്ഹൃത സംഖ്യകൾ സാധാരണഗതിയിൽ യൂറോപ്പിയൻ മരുന്നുകൾ നിയന്ത്രണ ഏജൻസി (EMA) നിർവഹിക്കുന്ന പ്രത്യേക സംവിധാനമായ EudraVigilance നിന്നാണ് ഉദ്ഭവിച്ചത്. EudraVigilance എന്നത് യൂറോപ്പിയൻ ഐക്യർജ്ജം (EEA) പ്രദേശത്ത് അനുമതി നൽകിയിരിക്കുന്ന മരുന്നുകളുടെ അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ റിപ്പോർട്ടുകൾ കേട്ടുകൊണ്ട് വിശകലനം നടത്തുന്ന സംവിധാനമാണ്. കോവിഡ്-19 വാക്സിനുകളുടെ വിതരണ ഘട്ടത്തിനു പുറമേ, EudraVigilance വാക്സിനേഷൻ ശേഷം റിപ്പോർട്ട് ചെയ്യപ്പെട്ട അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ നിരന്തര താളുകൾ പ്രസിദ്ധീകരിച്ചിരുന്നു, അതിൽ അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ സുരക്ഷിത ആശയങ്ങൾ ഉൾപ്പെടുന്നു, അതിൽ മരണം പോലും ഉൾപ്പെടുന്നു.

അതിനുപുറമേ, ഈ ഡാറ്റയുടെ താളുകളും അത് പ്രതിനിധികരിക്കുന്നതുമെന്ന് മനസ്സിലാക്കേണ്ടതുണ്ട്. EudraVigilance എന്നത് ഒരു പരോക്ഷ റിപ്പോർട്ടിംഗ് സംവിധാനമാണ്, അതിനർത്ഥം ആരും - ആരോഗ്യ പ്രവർത്തകർ, രോഗികൾ അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ജനങ്ങൾ - വാക്സിനേഷൻ ശേഷം ഉണ്ടായ എന്തെങ്കിലും മെഡിക്കൽ സംഭവങ്ങൾക്കെതിരെ റിപ്പോർട്ട് ചെയ്യാം. എന്നാൽ, റിപ്പോർട്ട് ഉണ്ടായിട്ടുള്ളത് വാക്സിനുകളാണ് അത് കാരണമായതാണെന്ന് ഉറപ്പാണ്. ഇത് "സംശയാസ്പദമായ" അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളാണ്, കാരണം പ്രാരംഭം ചെയ്യുമ്പോൾ കാരണം നിർണ്ണയിക്കുന്നില്ല. അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ കാരണങ്ങൾ അനേകം കാരണങ്ങളാണ്, അതിൽ ആശുപത്രി പ്രവർത്തനങ്ങളിൽ നിലനിൽക്കുന്ന അവസ്ഥകൾ, സംഭവിച്ച സാധാരണ രോഗങ്ങൾ അല്ലെങ്കിൽ അതിനു ബാധ്യതയില്ലാത്ത കാരണങ്ങൾ ഉൾപ്പെടുന്നു.

പ്രസ്താവന പറയുന്നത് 2021 മേയ് 19 ന് വരെ 10,570 മരണങ്ങൾ ഉണ്ടായിട്ടും 405,259 പക്ഷേപങ്ങൾ ഉണ്ടായിട്ടുമുണ്ടായിരുന്നു. ഈ സംഖ്യകൾ വാക്സിനുകളിൽ നിന്നും ഉണ്ടായ അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ കാരണം പ്രാമാണികമായ കേസുകളാണെന്ന് പ്രതിനിധികരിക്കുന്നതല്ല. ഇത് യൂറോപ്പിയൻ യൂണിയനിൽ വാക്സിനുകൾ നൽകിയത് മാത്രമല്ല, പകരം പല കോടികൾ വാക്സിനുകൾ നൽകിയിരുന്നു, പ്രായം കൂടിയവർ അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ആശുപത്രി പ്രവർത്തനങ്ങളിൽ നിലനിൽക്കുന്ന അവസ്ഥകളിൽ ഉള്ളവർക്ക് നൽകിയിരുന്നു, അത് മരണം ഉൾപ്പെടുന്ന പല ആരോഗ്യ സംഭവങ്ങളിലും അതിനു പുറമേ ഉള്ളതാണ്.

ഇതിനു പുറമേ, EMA പോലുള്ള നിയന്ത്രണ ഏജൻസികൾ അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ ഡാറ്റയും മറ്റ് വിവരങ്ങളും പരിശോധിച്ച് വാക്സിനേഷൻ അപകീർത്തിപ്പാടുകളുടെ പ്രത്യേക വിശദീകരണങ്ങളുടെ തരം തിരിച്ചറിയുകയും ചെയ്യുന്നു. പല റിപ്പോർട്ടുകളും വാക്സിനുകളാണ് അതിന് കാരണമായതാണെന്ന് കണ്ടെത്തിയിരുന്നു. ഒരു സാധ്യതയായ സുരക്ഷിത സവിശേഷത കണ്ടെത്തിയാൽ കൂടുതൽ അന്വേഷണം നടത്തുകയും, സുരക്ഷിതതയുടെ വിവരങ്ങൾ പരിശോധിക്കുകയും ചെയ്യും. ഉദാഹരണത്തിന്, ഒരു വാക്സിനുകളിൽ നിന്ന് ചെറിയ പക്ഷേപങ്ങൾ കണ്ടെത്തിയിരുന്നു, അതിന് അനുസൃതമായ സൂചനകൾ നൽകിയിരുന്നു, എന്നാൽ കോവിഡ്-19 വാക്സിനുകൾക്ക് ജനങ്ങൾക്ക് സുരക്ഷിതതയും പ്രായോഗിക പ്രാധാന്യവും ഉണ്ടായിരുന്നു എന്ന് തെളിയിച്ചു.

ഉപയോഗിച്ച വാർത്തയിലെ സംഖ്യകൾ 2021 മേയ് 19 ന് യൂറോപ്പിയൻ യൂണിയന്റെ പരിശോധന സംവിധാനത്തിൽ നിന്ന് അയച്ചു വന്ന പ്രായോഗിക റിപ്പോർട്ടുകളുടെ സത്യസന്ധത അനുസരിച്ചു സത്യമാണ്. എന്നാൽ, ഈ സംഖ്യകൾ വാക്സിനുകളുടെ കാരണമായ മരണങ്ങൾ അല്ലെങ്കിൽ പക്ഷേപങ്ങൾ ഉണ്ടായതാണെന്ന് തെറ്റായി പ്രസ്താവിച്ചിരിക്കുന്നു. വാക്സിനേഷൻ സംഭവത്തിന് കാരണമായി പരിശോധിക്കുന്ന പല സംഭവങ്ങൾക്കും കാരണം കണ്ടെത്താൻ സാധിച്ചിട്ടില്ല. കോവിഡ്-19 വാക്സിനുകൾ വിപുലമായ ക്ലിനിക്കൽ പരീക്ഷണങ്ങളും നിരന്തര പരിശോധനയും അനുഭവപ്പെടുത്തിയിട്ടുണ്ട്, അതിന്റെ ഫലം വാക്സിനുകളുടെ പ്രയോജനങ്ങൾ ആശങ്കകൾക്കേറെ അധികമാണ്. പൊതു ജനങ്ങൾക്ക് വാക്സിനുകളുടെ സുരക്ഷിതത കുറിച്ചുള്ള അറിവ് കൂടുതൽ വിശദമായ വിജ്ഞാന പരിശോധനയുടെ അടിസ്ഥാനത്തിൽ അടിസ്ഥാനപ്പെടുത്തേണ്ടതാണ്, അതിന്റെ പ്രായോഗിക റിപ്പോർട്ടുകളുടെ എണ്ണം അല്ല.

A recent social media post claims that Nick Janakis, a professor of pulmonology at the University of Crete, stated that the odds of developing thrombosis from the AstraZeneca vaccine are “not small.” This statement raises questions about the safety profile of the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine and whether the risk of thrombosis—a condition involving blood clots—is significant for those who receive it. To evaluate this claim, it is necessary to examine both what is known about the AstraZeneca vaccine and the context of expert commentary on vaccine safety.

The AstraZeneca vaccine, developed in collaboration with Oxford University, has been widely administered in many countries as part of the global effort to curtail the COVID-19 pandemic. In early 2021, reports emerged linking the vaccine to rare cases of thrombosis, particularly a type known as thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome (TTS), which combines blood clots with low platelet counts. These cases prompted several countries to temporarily pause or restrict the vaccine’s use, especially in younger adults, while health authorities investigated the risk.

Comprehensive reviews by regulatory bodies found that while there is an association between the AstraZeneca vaccine and rare clotting events, the absolute risk remains very low. For example, estimates generally suggest rates of approximately 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 vaccinated individuals, with the risk potentially higher in certain age groups and lower in others. The risk of developing thrombosis from the vaccine is therefore considered rare, although not zero.

The claim attributed to Professor Janakis—that the odds are "not small"—requires scrutiny. It is important to differentiate between a statistical risk that is rare but not negligible, and a risk that is “not small” in the sense of being common or frequent. Most medical authorities have characterized the risk as rare, with the benefits of vaccination outweighing the risks for the majority of people. However, some experts have voiced concerns about transparency and the need for careful risk communication, particularly for demographic groups found to have higher relative risk.

Further, there is limited public record of Professor Nick Janakis making the specific statement attributed to him. While it is plausible that experts would discuss the risks of vaccine-induced thrombosis, the characterization of the risk as “not small” does not align with the consensus among health authorities, which consistently describe the risk as rare. It is possible that the statement has been paraphrased or taken out of context, as experts sometimes refer to the importance of monitoring even rare adverse events closely, especially when vaccines are administered to millions of people.

In summary, the risk of developing thrombosis from the AstraZeneca vaccine exists, but it remains small in absolute terms. The phrase “not small,” as used in the social media post, overstates the risk compared to the prevailing scientific consensus. While vigilance and transparency are necessary, available data indicate that the odds of vaccine-induced thrombosis are rare, and the AstraZeneca vaccine continues to be recommended where its benefits outweigh the risks. The claim in the social media post is therefore misleading and lacks substantiation from authoritative sources or official statements from Professor Janakis.

A video circulating widely on social media claims to show protests in Spain sparked by public health measures implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic. The footage, which shows crowds gathered in public spaces, some holding banners and chanting, has prompted widespread discussion and debate online. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to analyze the video content, examine the context of protests in Spain during the pandemic, and determine whether the footage genuinely depicts demonstrations related to COVID-19 measures.

Spain, like many countries, implemented strict public health measures during the COVID-19 pandemic, including lockdowns, mask mandates, social distancing requirements, and restrictions on business operations. These measures, particularly during the first and second waves of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021, were met with a range of public reactions. While many citizens complied with government directives, there were instances of public dissent. Protests, though generally smaller in scale compared to those in some other European countries, did occur in various Spanish cities, often organized by groups opposing the economic impact of restrictions, mandatory mask usage, or vaccination campaigns.

Analysis of the viral video reveals several features that support the claim of it depicting protests in Spain. Language on banners and chants in the footage are in Spanish, and recognizable landmarks and signage suggest urban locations such as Madrid or Barcelona. In some cases, the banners reference freedom, anti-lockdown sentiments, or opposition to government-imposed restrictions, consistent with the messaging seen in actual demonstrations against COVID-19 measures in Spain during the pandemic.

However, it is important to note that not all protests in Spain during the pandemic were solely about public health measures. Some demonstrations were linked to broader political concerns, economic grievances, or calls for more government support. Furthermore, Spain saw protests during the pandemic on unrelated issues, such as labor rights or independence movements, which could be misattributed in viral content.

A key aspect of fact-checking such claims is verifying the date and context of the footage. Some earlier protest videos from Spain, particularly from May 2020, showed people rallying in cars or on balconies, while later demonstrations in 2021 featured more traditional street gatherings. The viral video’s depiction of mask usage and crowd size can help pinpoint the likely period within the pandemic when the protest occurred, as regulations and public behavior shifted over time.

In conclusion, available evidence suggests that the viral video does indeed show protests in Spain related to public health measures instituted during the COVID-19 pandemic. The visual cues, language, and protest themes align with documented demonstrations that took place in response to government restrictions. However, as with all viral content, viewers should be cautious and consider the specific context and timing of such footage, as protest scenes can sometimes be repurposed or misrepresented online. Fact-checking and analysis remain crucial in discerning the true origins and motivations behind viral social media content.

A widely circulated social media post claims that blood donated by individuals vaccinated with mRNA COVID-19 vaccines is “genetically altered and polluted,” rendering such donations unsafe. This assertion has raised concerns among some members of the public regarding the safety of the blood supply and the impact of COVID-19 vaccines on donor blood. A thorough examination of the science and blood donation protocols, however, reveals that this claim is unfounded.

COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, such as those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, work by delivering a small piece of genetic material known as messenger RNA (mRNA) into the body’s cells. This mRNA instructs the cells to produce a harmless piece of the virus’s spike protein, which then triggers an immune response. Importantly, the mRNA from the vaccine does not integrate into the recipient’s DNA or alter their genetic code. The mRNA fragment is rapidly broken down and eliminated from the body within a few days after vaccination.

Blood donation organizations around the world, including those in the United States and Europe, continue to accept blood from individuals who have received mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. These organizations have established protocols to ensure the safety of the blood supply. Donors who have received an mRNA vaccine are eligible to give blood as long as they are feeling well and meet other standard eligibility criteria. There is no evidence to suggest that blood donated by vaccinated individuals poses any health risk to recipients.

The claim that vaccinated blood is “genetically altered” misrepresents how mRNA vaccines work. The mRNA in the vaccine does not remain in the bloodstream or get incorporated into the genetic material of blood cells. It serves as a temporary set of instructions for the body to recognize and fight the coronavirus. Once its job is done, the mRNA degrades naturally and is removed from the body.

Additionally, the suggestion that vaccinated blood is “polluted” has no scientific basis. The components introduced by the mRNA vaccines do not linger in the blood and cannot be transmitted through blood transfusion. Health authorities and transfusion experts have found no difference in safety between blood from vaccinated and unvaccinated donors.

Misinformation about blood donation and vaccination can have serious consequences by discouraging both blood donors and recipients, potentially leading to shortages and impacting patient care. Medical experts emphasize that the blood donation process remains safe and that available scientific evidence does not support the notion that COVID-19 vaccination “alters” or “pollutes” blood.

In summary, the claim that blood from mRNA COVID-19 vaccine recipients is genetically altered or unsafe is not supported by current scientific understanding or blood safety protocols. Blood from vaccinated individuals is considered safe for transfusion, and vaccination status does not impact the genetic integrity or safety of donated blood.

Analiz komplè pou sijans ak protokol donasyon sèl kouvri, men, revelè ke afirman sa a pa fonde.

Vaksin ARNm pou COVID-19, tankou sa yo ki te fèt pa Pfizer-BioNTech ak Moderna, travay yo pase yon piti peryò genetik yo kote ARNm (ARNm) nan sèl yo. ARNm sa a instruksyon sèl yo pou pèpare yon piti peryò senp nan proteiny spike virus la, ki fèt yon repons imounè. Men, pou yon piti peryò, ARNm nan vaksin sa a pa integre nan ADN pèson yo oswa alòte kòdi genetik yo. Peryò ARNm sa a te detèse rapi ak elimine nan yon piti peryò aprè vaksinasyon.

Organizasyon donasyon sèl kouvri nan tout mondi, tankou sa yo nan Etazini ak Ewrop, k ap pase sèl kouvri nan moun ki te resevwa vaksin ARNm pou COVID-19. Sa yo te etabli protokol pou sètite sèl kouvri. Donatè yo ki te resevwa vaksin ARNm k ap pase sèl kouvri si yo fèt bon ak k ap pase kriterye standart lòt yo. Pa gen evedans pou sugere ke sèl kouvri nan moun ki te vaksine fè yon ris piblik pou reseptè.

Afiyansyon ke sèl kouvri nan moun ki te vaksine te altere genetikman mispresante kèk vaksin ARNm travay. ARNm nan vaksin sa a pa reste nan sèl kouvri oswa te integre nan materyè genetik sèl kouvri. Aprè kòm yo fèt, ARNm sa a detèse natirèlman ak elimine nan yon piti peryò.

Anplisèman, sugerye ke sèl kouvri nan moun ki te vaksine te polye pa gen baze sijans. Komponan yo ki te fèt pa vaksin ARNm pa reste nan sèl kouvri ak pa kapab transmete par transfuzyon sèl kouvri. Autorite sanèt ak eksipè transfuzyon te gen yon diferans piblik ant sèl kouvri nan moun ki te vaksine ak moun ki pa te vaksine.

Mispren sou donasyon sèl kouvri ak vaksinasyon kapab fè yon konsekans serè pou dekouraje moun ki don sèl kouvri ak moun ki resepte, kapab fè yon manki ak pèt kare pase maladie yo. Eksipè sanèt pèmèt ke proses donasyon sèl kouvri toujou sèk ak ke evedans sijans ki gen pa pèmèt notasyon ke vaksinasyon pou COVID-19 te altere oswa polye sèl kouvri.

Anplisèman, afiryansyon ke sèl kouvri nan moun ki te resevwa vaksin ARNm pou COVID-19 te altere genetikman oswa te sèk pa pèmèt pa konnen sijans kounye a ak protokol sètite sèl kouvri. A recent social media post claims that "The Red Cross does not accept blood from people vaccinated for the COVID-19." This assertion has gained traction online, fueling confusion and concern among individuals wishing to donate blood in the wake of widespread COVID-19 vaccination campaigns. A close examination of this claim, including official policies and broader donation guidelines, reveals that the statement is misleading and does not accurately reflect current blood donation practices.

The American Red Cross and other major blood collection organizations have played a critical role throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, both in supporting patients and in managing supplies during periods of heightened demand. As vaccinations became widely available, questions naturally arose regarding whether recently vaccinated individuals could safely donate blood and whether their blood would be accepted by major blood banks.

Fact-checking the claim begins with a review of the Red Cross’s official stance. The Red Cross has stated publicly that individuals who have received a COVID-19 vaccine are eligible to donate blood, provided they feel well and meet standard donation criteria. The only stipulation is that potential donors must know which vaccine they received, as this information is requested during the donation process. There are minor deferral periods for some vaccines, typically only if the donor is unsure which vaccine they received or if they received a live attenuated vaccine—a type not used for COVID-19 in the United States. For the widely administered Pfizer, Moderna, and Johnson & Johnson vaccines, no deferral period is required unless the donor feels unwell.

This policy is based on scientific consensus and recommendations from health authorities, who have found no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines adversely affect blood donation or recipients. The vaccine components do not remain in the bloodstream and do not pose any risk to those receiving transfusions. The Red Cross and other blood collection agencies have consistently communicated that the need for blood donations remains urgent, regardless of vaccination status, and that vaccinated individuals are encouraged to donate.

The origins of the misinformation may stem from early confusion around new vaccines or from misunderstandings about standard deferral practices for certain illnesses or vaccinations. In some cases, temporary deferral periods are imposed after receiving specific vaccines or treatments, but these precautions are not unique to COVID-19 vaccines and are in place to ensure donor safety and accurate health records. Additionally, the Red Cross has clarified that they do not label, separate, or reject blood based on COVID-19 vaccination status.

In summary, the claim that "The Red Cross does not accept blood from people vaccinated for the COVID-19" is false. Individuals who have received a COVID-19 vaccine are eligible to donate blood, provided they are healthy and meet basic requirements. The Red Cross continues to encourage all eligible donors, vaccinated or not, to participate in blood donation drives to support patients in need. Misinformation about blood donation policies can have real-world consequences, potentially discouraging donors and impacting blood supply. As such, it is important to seek information from reputable sources and verify claims before sharing them online.

A social media post has claimed that more than 4,000 deaths in the United States have resulted from COVID-19 vaccines. This assertion has circulated widely, fueling concerns and debates about vaccine safety. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to examine the available data, the reporting systems in place, and the context surrounding vaccine-related adverse events.

The primary source for information about vaccine side effects and deaths in the US is the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), which is managed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). VAERS is an open, passive surveillance system that allows anyone—including healthcare providers, patients, and family members—to report any health event occurring after vaccination, regardless of causality. This system is designed to act as an early warning tool for potential safety concerns.

Since the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines in December 2020, VAERS has received thousands of reports of deaths following vaccination. These reports have often been cited in social media posts, such as the claim that more than 4,000 deaths have occurred due to the vaccines. However, it is crucial to understand what these reports actually indicate. A report submitted to VAERS does not mean that the vaccine caused the death; it simply records that a death occurred after vaccination. The CDC and FDA investigate serious events, including deaths, to determine whether there is a plausible link to the vaccine.

The majority of people who have received COVID-19 vaccines are older adults or individuals with underlying health conditions—populations who are statistically more likely to experience health events, including death, within any given timeframe. When reviewing the reported deaths, health officials examine medical records, autopsy results, and other data to assess causality. So far, thorough reviews have found that most deaths reported after vaccination were due to causes unrelated to the vaccine, such as heart disease, cancer, or COVID-19 itself.

There have been rare instances where a causal relationship was established between a COVID-19 vaccine and a fatal outcome, such as severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) or blood clotting disorders associated with certain vaccines, but these cases are exceedingly uncommon. The CDC continues to monitor and investigate these rare adverse events, updating guidance as new information becomes available.

In summary, while more than 4,000 deaths may have been reported to VAERS following COVID-19 vaccination, this number does not represent confirmed vaccine-caused deaths. The data are subject to misinterpretation, as reports include any death after vaccination, regardless of cause. Rigorous analysis by health authorities has found that COVID-19 vaccines approved for use in the US are overwhelmingly safe and effective, with the benefits far outweighing the risks for the vast majority of individuals. Public health experts caution against misrepresenting VAERS data and urge individuals to rely on thoroughly vetted information when making decisions about vaccination.

Главни извор информација о нежелих ефектима и смртима у Сједињеним Државама је система Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), управљен од стране Центра за контролу и предупредње за болести (CDC) и Фудзина и лекарства (FDA). Већина људи који су добили коронавирусне вакцине су старији или имају претходне здравствене проблеме – популације које статистички имају већу вероватноћу да изразе здравствене епизоде, укључујући смрт, у било којем тренутку. Када се процени смрт, здравствени служби прегледају медицинске записи, аутопсе и друге податке да би проценили узрок. Досад, тежи прегледи су пронашли да је већина смрти након вакцинације изазвана причињама неповезаним са вакцином, као што су сердечне болести, рак или коронавирус сам по себи.

Имало је ретки случајеви где је утврђена веза између коронавирусне вакцине и смртног исхода, као што су тешке алергичне реакције (анфилаксија) или крвареће поремећaje повезани са одређеним вакцинама, али су ови случајеви изузетно ретки. Строга анализа здравствених организација је пронашла да су коронавирусне вакцине одобрено за коришћење у Сједињеним Државама веома безбедне и ефикасне, са користим значајно већом од ризика за већину људи. Claims that individuals vaccinated for COVID-19 have become “human magnets,” able to attract metal objects to their skin, have circulated widely on social media since early in the vaccination campaign. Proponents of this theory suggest that ingredients in the vaccines, such as microchips, nanotechnology, or metallic compounds, render vaccinated people magnetic. This article examines the origins of the claim, its scientific plausibility, and the evidence available.

The origin of the “magnetism” claim can be traced to viral videos and anecdotes shared online, where individuals demonstrate coins, keys, or other metallic objects apparently sticking to their skin after vaccination. These videos often frame this as evidence of a hidden agenda or unknown side effects associated with COVID-19 vaccines.

To assess this claim, it is important to review how COVID-19 vaccines work and what ingredients they contain. The most widely used COVID-19 vaccines, including those from Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, and Johnson & Johnson, rely on mRNA or viral vector technology. Their ingredients lists are publicly available and include substances like lipids, salts, sugars, and stabilizers. None of these vaccines contain metals, magnetic materials, or microchips. Even vaccines that use adjuvants (which are not present in mRNA vaccines) do not use magnetic substances.

From a scientific perspective, human magnetism is not possible through vaccination. The body does not develop magnetic properties by the introduction of biological or chemical substances at the minuscule quantities found in vaccines. For an object to become noticeably magnetized, it must contain ferromagnetic materials like iron, nickel, or cobalt, none of which are present in COVID-19 vaccines.

Demonstrations of objects sticking to skin are typically explained by basic physics and skin properties. Skin can be slightly moist or oily, allowing lightweight objects to adhere via surface tension or natural stickiness. This phenomenon, sometimes referred to as the “spoon trick,” has been performed for decades using non-magnetic materials, with no relation to vaccination status.

Additionally, reports from health professionals and vaccine recipients worldwide have not documented magnetism as a side effect in any credible medical literature. Regulatory agencies such as the Food and Drug Administration and the World Health Organization have explicitly stated that COVID-19 vaccines do not cause magnetism.

In summary, the claim that COVID-19 vaccination turns people into “human magnets” is not supported by scientific evidence or the known composition of the vaccines. Demonstrations of objects adhering to skin are easily explained by natural skin properties rather than any effect of vaccination. Health authorities continue to monitor and assess vaccine safety, and no credible data supports the human magnetism claim. The spread of this misinformation highlights the importance of relying on verified scientific information when evaluating health-related claims.

article_content:
A viral social media post claims that authorities can determine whether someone has received a COVID-19 vaccine using a “special camera” that detects metallic nanoparticles and luciferase allegedly present in the vaccines. According to the post, this technology would allow officials to identify people using fake vaccination certificates. This article examines the accuracy of these claims and explores the science behind the components mentioned.

Understanding the Claim

The post’s core assertion hinges on two elements: first, that COVID-19 vaccines contain metallic nanoparticles and luciferase, and second, that a specialized camera can detect these substances in vaccinated individuals. The implication is that authorities have a means of visually scanning people to confirm vaccination status, potentially exposing those with fraudulent documentation.

Background: COVID-19 Vaccines and Their Ingredients

COVID-19 vaccines, including those from Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, Johnson & Johnson, and AstraZeneca, have gone through rigorous regulatory review for both safety and transparency regarding their ingredients. The core components of these vaccines include messenger RNA (mRNA) or viral vectors, lipids (fats), salts, sugars, and stabilizing agents. None of the authorized COVID-19 vaccines contain “metallic nanoparticles” in the context implied by the post.

The mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles—microscopic fat bubbles—to protect and deliver genetic material into cells. These are not metals and are rapidly broken down and cleared by the body. They are not detectable by any camera or imaging technology outside of laboratory environments and certainly not in a way that would allow for scanning people for vaccination status.

Luciferase: What Is It?

Luciferase is an enzyme found in fireflies and some other organisms that enables bioluminescence. In laboratory research, luciferase is sometimes used as a marker to visualize whether a gene has been taken up by cells, but it is not an ingredient in any approved COVID-19 vaccine for humans. While luciferase may be used in preclinical animal studies to track vaccine uptake, this is not the case for the vaccines administered to the general public.

Fact-Checking the Camera Claim

There is no evidence of any camera or scanning device capable of detecting either metallic nanoparticles or luciferase in the human body as a means of confirming COVID-19 vaccination. Medical imaging technology such as X-rays, MRI, or specialized laboratory equipment can detect certain substances, but these tools are not portable, are not designed for mass screening, and cannot detect vaccine components in the way described. Additionally, the substances mentioned are not present in the vaccines to begin with.

Furthermore, official methods for verifying vaccination status rely on documentation, such as vaccination cards and digital records, not on bodily scans. If authorities need to verify vaccine records, they check databases and paperwork, not physical markers inside the body.

Conclusion

The claim that authorities can use a special camera to check for metallic nanoparticles and luciferase in COVID-19 vaccines to identify fake certificates is false. COVID-19 vaccines do not contain metallic nanoparticles or luciferase, and no such scanning technology exists for this purpose. The spread of misinformation about vaccine ingredients and surveillance methods can cause unnecessary alarm, and it is important to rely on verified scientific information and official sources regarding vaccines and public health measures.

article_content:
In December 2020, claims began circulating on social media that French professor Jean-Bernard Fourtillan was abducted from his home, had his phone confiscated, and was forcibly admitted to the isolation ward of a psychiatric clinic because he criticized the COVID-19 vaccines. This narrative quickly gained traction among groups skeptical of public health measures and vaccines, prompting widespread concern and speculation about government overreach and the suppression of dissenting scientific voices. A closer examination of the facts, however, reveals a more nuanced reality.

Jean-Bernard Fourtillan, a retired professor of pharmacology, became a notable figure in France for his outspoken views on COVID-19 and vaccines. He promoted several controversial theories regarding the virus, its origins, and the safety of vaccines. In particular, Fourtillan was known for making unsubstantiated claims about vaccine dangers and for his involvement in promoting unapproved medical treatments.

According to reports from December 2020, Fourtillan was indeed involuntarily admitted to a psychiatric facility, the Centre Hospitalier Le Mas Careiron in Uzès, France. However, the circumstances surrounding his hospitalization are more complex than the social media post suggests. French authorities did not abduct Professor Fourtillan in the sense of a covert or extrajudicial action. article_content:
A social media post circulating online claims that a new medical study has proven the spike protein produced by COVID-19 vaccines causes damage to blood vessels and leads to thrombosis. This claim taps into ongoing concerns and misinformation regarding the safety of COVID-19 vaccines, particularly those that use messenger RNA (mRNA) technology to instruct cells to produce a version of the coronavirus spike protein and trigger an immune response.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to understand how COVID-19 vaccines work, the nature of the spike protein, and what current scientific research indicates regarding vaccine safety and risks.

COVID-19 vaccines developed by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna utilize mRNA technology. Upon injection, the mRNA enters cells and instructs them to produce a harmless piece of the coronavirus spike protein. The immune system recognizes this protein as foreign and mounts a defense, preparing the body to fight off future infections. The spike protein produced after vaccination is similar to, but not identical with, the spike protein found on the surface of the actual virus.

Concerns about the spike protein’s effects emerged early in the pandemic, as some research suggested the spike protein could play a role in the vascular complications observed in severe COVID-19 cases. However, it is important to distinguish between the spike protein generated during infection and the controlled production induced by the vaccine. In COVID-19 infection, the virus multiplies extensively, producing large amounts of spike protein as it damages cells and tissues. Vaccine-induced spike protein is produced in much smaller quantities and does not replicate or spread in the same way.

The claim that a new medical study "proved" the vaccine spike protein causes blood vessel damage and thrombosis is not supported by the consensus of current scientific evidence. While isolated laboratory studies have examined the effects of spike protein on cells in a dish, these studies do not replicate the conditions found in vaccinated individuals. Real-world data from millions of vaccine recipients show that serious adverse events, including blood clots (thrombosis), are exceedingly rare and occur at much lower rates than those associated with COVID-19 infection itself.

Safety monitoring systems in various countries have detected rare cases of blood clots associated with certain vaccines, notably the AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson vaccines, which use a different technology (viral vectors) than mRNA vaccines. These rare events led to additional research, updated guidelines, and in some cases, restrictions on use in certain populations. For mRNA vaccines, the risk of thrombosis remains extremely low, and no definitive evidence links the spike protein produced by these vaccines to widespread vascular damage.

In summary, while ongoing research continues to monitor vaccine safety, there is no scientific consensus or credible study that proves the spike protein produced by COVID-19 vaccines damages blood vessels and leads to thrombosis. Such claims misrepresent preliminary laboratory findings and real-world safety data. The benefits of COVID-19 vaccination in preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death far outweigh the very rare risks of adverse events. It remains essential to rely on established health authorities and peer-reviewed research when evaluating vaccine safety claims.

article_content:
A recent social media post has gone viral, claiming that Russian scientists successfully extracted a “5g nanochip” from the Pfizer/BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine and published its schematics. This claim has sparked renewed concern and debate among vaccine skeptics and the wider public. As misinformation continues to circulate online, it is crucial to critically assess such statements and provide clear, evidence-based analysis.

The claim suggests that a sophisticated piece of technology—a nanochip allegedly capable of interfacing with 5G networks—was discovered inside a widely distributed vaccine. According to the post, Russian researchers not only found this device but also released detailed design schematics, implying a vast and coordinated conspiracy at the heart of the global COVID-19 vaccination effort.

To evaluate this assertion, it's important to understand the composition and manufacturing process of the Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine. This vaccine utilizes messenger RNA (mRNA) technology, which instructs cells to produce a protein similar to the spike protein found on the surface of the coronavirus, thereby triggering an immune response. The vaccine’s ingredients include mRNA, lipids to encapsulate the RNA, salts, sugars, and stabilizing agents. Detailed ingredient lists are publicly available and have been scrutinized by independent experts, regulatory agencies, and governments worldwide.

Nanochips, particularly those capable of interacting with telecommunications infrastructure like 5G, are complex electronic devices. They require multiple components such as semiconductors, antennas, power sources, and processors—none of which could be miniaturized to the scale necessary to fit inside a vaccine’s microscopic droplets. Additionally, manufacturing such devices in the billions, as vaccine doses have been produced, would present enormous logistical, technical, and financial challenges, making the claim highly implausible.

The assertion that Russian scientists extracted such a nanochip and published its schematics lacks credible support. No reputable scientific institution in Russia or elsewhere has published studies or reports confirming the existence of electronic microdevices in COVID-19 vaccines. Major news outlets, peer-reviewed journals, and international health organizations have not reported any such findings. Schematics purportedly showing “nanochips” have circulated in the past, but these images are often found to be unrelated to vaccine technology, frequently sourced from generic electronics or even fictional designs.

It is important to recognize that claims about “microchips” or “nanochips” in vaccines have been a persistent theme among misinformation campaigns since the beginning of the pandemic. These narratives often play on public fears about surveillance and government control. However, such theories have repeatedly been debunked by scientific experts, and no credible evidence has ever surfaced to support them.

In conclusion, the claim that Russian scientists extracted a 5g nanochip from the Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine and published its schematics is unfounded and unsupported by scientific evidence. The composition of the vaccine is well documented, and the logistics and science behind inserting functional nanochips into vaccine doses are not feasible with current technology. This claim appears to be another iteration of persistent misinformation surrounding COVID-19 vaccines.

Недавний пост в социальных сетях стал вирусным, утверждая, что российские ученые успешно извлекли «наночип 5G» из вакцины Pfizer/BioNTech от COVID-19 и опубликовали его схемы. Это заявление вызвало новое беспокойство и дискуссии среди скептиков вакцинации и широкой публики. В условиях продолжения распространения дезинформации в интернете важно критически оценить подобные утверждения и предоставить четкий, основанной на доказательствах анализ.

Согласно заявлению, в широко распространенной вакцине был обнаружен сложный технологический элемент — наночип, якобы способный взаимодействовать с сетями 5G. По мнению поста, российские исследователи не только нашли этот устройство, но и опубликовали подробные схемы, что подразумевает масштабную и организованную схему, лежащую в основе глобальных усилий по вакцинации от COVID-19.

Для оценки этого утверждения важно понимать состав и производственный процесс вакцины Pfizer/BioNTech. Эта вакцина использует технологию мРНК, которая инструктирует клетки производить белок, похожий на шиповидный белок, найденный на поверхности коронавируса, тем самым вызывая иммунный ответ. Компоненты вакцины включают мРНК, липиды для упаковки РНК, соли, сахара и стабилизаторы. Подробные списки ингредиентов публично доступны и были проверены независимыми экспертами, регулирующими органами и правительствами по всему миру.

Наночипы, особенно те, которые способны взаимодействовать с телекоммуникационной инфраструктурой, такой как 5G, представляют собой сложные электронные устройства. Они требуют множества компонентов, таких как полупроводники, антенны, источники питания и процессоры — ни один из которых не может быть миниатюризирован до такой степени, чтобы поместиться в микроскопические капли вакцины. Кроме того, производство таких устройств в миллиардах, как это было при производстве доз вакцины, предъявляет огромные логистические, технические и финансовые требования, что делает утверждение чрезвычайно маловероятным.

Утверждение о том, что российские ученые извлекли такой наночип и опубликовали его схемы, не имеет достоверной поддержки. Никакой уважаемой научной организации в России или где-либо еще не опубликовала исследования или отчеты, подтверждающие существование электронных микроустройств в вакцинах от COVID-19. Основные средства массовой информации, рецензируемые журналы и международные организации здравоохранения не сообщали о таких находках. Изображения, якобы показывающие «наночипы», в прошлом также распространялись, но эти картинки часто оказывались несвязанными с технологией вакцин, часто получены из общей электроники или даже из вымышленных дизайнов.

Важно признать, что утверждения о «микрочипах» или «наночипах» в вакцинах стали постоянной темой дезинформации с момента начала пандемии. Эти нарративы часто играют на страхах населения относительно наблюдения и контроля со стороны государства. Однако такие теории многократно опровергались научными экспертами, и до сих пор не было найдено достоверных доказательств их подтверждения.

В заключение, утверждение о том, что российские ученые извлекли наночип 5G из вакцины Pfizer/BioNTech и опубликовали его схемы, не имеет оснований и не подтверждается научными данными. Состав вакцины хорошо документирован, и логистика и наука введения функциональных наночипов в дозы вакцины не представляют собой возможности современной технологии. Это утверждение, похоже, является еще одной версией постоянной дезинформации, связанной с вакцинами от COVID-19.

article_content:
A recent social media post asserts that, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), COVID-19 vaccines are "experimental." This claim has circulated widely since the initial rollout of vaccines in late 2020 and early 2021, leading to confusion and concern among the public about the safety and efficacy of these vaccines. A careful examination of the claim and the context surrounding vaccine development and regulatory approval can clarify whether the WHO has explicitly designated COVID-19 vaccines as experimental.

First, it is important to understand the process by which vaccines are developed and approved for use. Vaccine development typically involves several phases: preclinical studies, followed by Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 clinical trials. These trials are designed to assess safety, immune response, dosage, and efficacy in increasingly larger groups of volunteers. COVID-19 vaccines underwent these rigorous phases, albeit on accelerated timelines due to the urgent global need. Regulatory agencies, such as the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA), and others, reviewed the data from these trials before granting Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) or, in some cases, full approval.

The term "experimental" refers to medical interventions that are still in the research phase, typically not yet proven to be safe or effective in humans outside of tightly controlled clinical trials. Once a medical product passes through all necessary phases of testing and receives authorization from regulatory agencies for public use, it is no longer considered experimental. Instead, it is labeled as "authorized" or "approved," depending on the regulatory pathway.

The World Health Organization played a central role during the pandemic in providing guidance and information about COVID-19 vaccines. The WHO maintains lists of vaccines that have received Emergency Use Listing (EUL), a process that evaluates vaccines for quality, safety, and efficacy for global use, especially in countries lacking robust regulatory systems. The WHO's communications and official statements clearly refer to COVID-19 vaccines authorized for emergency or general use—not as experimental products.

The confusion likely arises from the emergency nature of the initial vaccine rollouts. Emergency Use Authorization or Emergency Use Listing allows vaccines to be distributed and administered based on available evidence, prior to full licensure, in order to address public health emergencies. However, by the time vaccines are authorized for emergency use, they have already undergone substantial testing in tens of thousands of participants. The WHO and other regulatory bodies have not labeled the COVID-19 vaccines as experimental; rather, they have described them as safe and effective, while continuing to monitor for any rare adverse effects as distribution scales up.

In conclusion, the claim that the World Health Organization has explicitly stated COVID-19 vaccines are experimental is inaccurate. The WHO has not referred to these vaccines as experimental and has instead endorsed their use based on scientific evidence and international regulatory review. While ongoing monitoring and data collection continue, as is standard with any new medical product, the COVID-19 vaccines distributed under emergency or full authorization are not experimental by any recognized medical or regulatory standard. This distinction is critical for public understanding and confidence in the global vaccination effort.
